description: Topic: Fire behavior in microgravity (space) is fundamentally different from Earth. NASA has collected real combustion experiment data from the ISS. The goal is to use AI to extract meaningful fire safety insights from this data to protect astronauts and spacecraft.
summary:
Fire behaves differently in microgravity, making fire safety a major challenge for future space missions. Although NASA has conducted decades of combustion experiments, finding and comparing their results can be difficult.

Flame in Freefall is an interactive research dashboard that brings NASA's microgravity combustion investigations into one place. It helps users explore experiments relevant to spacecraft, Moon habitats, and Mars missions, compare their conditions, and understand which areas still lack experimental data.

The platform also includes a paper-based question-answering feature with citations, data exports for further analysis, and an experimental modeling section. Rather than presenting uncertain predictions as facts, it highlights limitations and explains what current research can and cannot tell us.

Our goal is to make existing combustion research easier to explore and help researchers identify the knowledge gaps that matter for safer human exploration beyond Earth.
details:
Flame in Freefall was developed to address an important challenge in human space exploration: understanding and managing fire risks in environments where flames behave differently from those on Earth.

We built an interactive dashboard that brings together NASA microgravity combustion investigation information and experimental data, making it easier to explore research relevant to spacecraft, Moon habitats, and Mars missions.

The dashboard allows users to rank investigations for different habitat conditions, understand why each investigation receives its ranking, visualize oxygen concentration and pressure ranges, and compare experiments side by side. It also includes a question-answering feature designed to retrieve information from research papers with numbered citations, along with data export functionality for further analysis.

Another important part of our project is identifying what existing research does not yet cover. The platform highlights missing experimental conditions, including partial-gravity research gaps, helping users understand where further investigation may be needed.

We developed the application using Python, Streamlit, SQLite, pandas, NumPy, Plotly, and scikit-learn. The system includes data validation, investigation ranking, source-based retrieval, an experimental machine-learning model, and validation checks.

What makes our approach meaningful is its emphasis on transparency. Instead of presenting predictions as established scientific conclusions, we show the assumptions behind our rankings, explain the limitations of the available data, and distinguish experimental modeling from verified safety guidance.

Our aim is to make NASA combustion research easier to access, understand, and build upon, contributing to safer and more informed decisions for future human exploration beyond Earth.
